items.title: USA Today Co. blames AI for its revenue woes. It also sees AI as a solution. - Poynter
items.summary:
USA Today Co. is also using AI to expand its video offerings, allowing it to grow video advertising, said Reed. The company aims to make all of its content available in video as well as text. It has also started creating branded advertising content on its platform that is AI-discoverable. [...] To build that foundation, USA Today Co. is cutting costs and leaning on AI. One of those initiatives is its controversial partnership with technology company Palantir, which USA Today Co. first announced in August. That deal has allowed the company to use AI-powered tools from Palantir to analyze data from customers and readers and identify ways to monetize them. Though unions at dozens of USA Today Co. newspapers have decried the partnership, Reed said the first “products” are now live and [...] “Because there’s so much crap and untrusted content out there on the AI platforms, it’s a real opportunity for us to partner with brands to create trusted messaging and to make that discoverable on AI platforms,” Reed said. 

Before the end of the year, USA Today Co. plans to announce “at least one, possibly two” more content licensing deals with AI companies — another source of revenue, Reed said.

In June 1945, two months before the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Japan, a group of Manhattan Project scientists warned that, without an international agreement limiting the manufacture and use of nuclear weapons, humanity could face “total mutual destruction.”

Today, some tech and legal scholars believe we are at a similar turning point with artificial intelligence — and that without prompt regulation, humankind might again be in peril.
